Nelson, whose name will ever live first in naval story, and the Duke of Wi llincton, the conqueror at Waterloo, met once, and but once, in the course of their eventful lives. The meeting is thus detailed in the article on the Life of Howe. þÿ last number of the Edinburgh Review, in the A orfu/k Beji con. þÿ Having here incidentally mentioned the Duke of Wellington and Nelson together, it may not be uninteresting to our readers to learn that they met once, and but once, and then bv mere accident. The Duke, then Sir Arthur Wellesley, had just returned from his ever-memorablc campaign in India; but his fame;, though high amongst all those who knew any thing of the concerns ol that remote region, had not yet become so familiar to the mass of society at home as to render it profitable to the print-sellers and tavern keepþÿ ers to exhibit his physiognomy to the public gaze. Consequently, the features, now so familiar to all, weie then so little known þÿ even to Nelson þÿ that when he found himself one day in the waiting room of one ol the Secretaries of Stale in company with the great Eastern warrior, he knew him not. It wasiotherwise. with Nelson, whose deeds, having been performed nearer home, were far better, or, at all events, more generally known; and wiih whose appearance Sir Arthur could not hut he well acquainted, even had he had no other help than the signs over the inn-doors 00 his way from Ports mouth. The natural attraction of ge nius drew them together, and the Minister whose

leisure they were waiting for being long engaged, these two illustrious men were left in conversation for some time. The news of Sir Robert þÿ( alder s action had just been received, and this naturally formed a principal topic of their discourse. þÿ ley said to Lord Nelson þÿ This measure of Sir Arthur Wellessuccess þÿwon do t now-a days, for your Lordship has taught the public to expect something more þÿbrilliant. Shortly alter tins remark, Lord Nelson left the waiting-room, evidently to find out who his new friend was. and, returning in a minute, renewed the conversation on a Ircsh fooling. Nelson had at that time some project for occupying Sardinia, and he wished Sir Arthur to take charge of the troops on the occasion. But he replied that lie would rather not þÿ that lie had just returned from India þÿ in short, he did not enter into that view Soon afterwards, Lord Nelson Sailed þÿ the battle of Trafalgar was fought þÿ and they never met þÿagain.

St. Croix, Christiansled, January 7th 1839. e+;» Tlie mails pr. first December packet were yesterday received. The Lin r I of Durham arrived at Portsmouth November 28th in the Inconstant frigate from Quebec. Tempestuous weather prevailed in the channel the latter part of November. The new insurrection in Canada was not known in England on the 30th Novemlxtr. The English and Turkish fleets had separated; the former having gone to Malta and the latter to Smyrna. In the east, military operations on a great scale were progressing ; 25.000 British troops were marching from Bombay to oppose the progress of the Persians towards the British possessions. The whole military force of the three Presidencies in India under the British Government are -estimated at 200,000 men, of which 30,000 are Europeans. It is s aid ihat the 10,000 British troopsquartered in Ireland, are to be ordered on foreign service, and are to be replaced by English militia regiments. Much activity prevailed in the Naval Dock yards in England.

We have received New York gazettes, of the 15th ultimo. A new attempt at Invasion had been made from Detroit to Ainherstberg Upper Canada, of a few hundred malcontents- They are said to have destroyed an English Steamer and some property. General Brady of the U. S. army was actively engaged in preventing these incursions ; he had seized a considerable quantity of concealed arms and ammunition belonging to the insurrectionists.

AFFAIRS OF RUSSIA. A letter from St. Petersburg of the 15th in the Courrier Prancais, has the following: þÿ " Two aids-de-camp of the Emperor, charged by His Majesty with missions from the Cabinet, quitted this day for Odessa, from which place one of them will immediately proceed to Constantinople. The English ambassy has dispatched three coutiers within -48 hours: The subject of t he mission is the entirely new turn which the affairs of Turkey have taken, and the danger apprehended from the passage of the Dardanelles by a British squadron, all of which was wholly unexpected by his Majesty. Sultan Mahmond is called Upon to give a categorical explanation. Extraordinary measures arc in preparation as to

the armies of ihe north and Bessarabia, also as to the corps of embarkation and the fleet of the Black Sea. If England should send Iter fleet into the Dardanelles, the Egyptian army would invade Anatolia, wheie the Turkish troops are unable to oppose effectual resistance At all events, this conflict must sooner or later ensue, and although Russia will not accelerate matters, it w ill not recoil from war, rather than lose its position. " The news from Caucasus shows that affairs are still more complicated, not because the Russian troops have been defeated in several engagements, but because it is proved that succour is regularly organised at Constantinople, at Si nope, and at Trebizonde, by English agents, whereby the resistance of t lie Caucasus may be interminably prolonged, and even Georgia may be compromised by the contagion of rebellion. The Tcherkeses have among them a multitude of European officers, who teach them to turn their local advantages to account ; and the native princes who might have been gradually won over to the cause of Russia, can no longer treat with the Cabinet without exposing themselves to certain death. The blockade, which does more injury to the commerce of Russian subjects than to that of the insurgent Caucasians, and which is very expensive, cannot be continued during the had season, whereas the coasting vessels can at all times convey to the rebels the supplies of which I have just spoken. The army of the Ivouban and the Cossacks have been re-

modelled thrice without giving consistency to the Russian forces in that quarter, and t he generals will again be changed to as little purpose as heretofore. This war is a cankerworm to the empire." The envoy lo ihe United Slates, who was appointed previously to the last voyage of the Emperor is about to proceed on his mission- The Cabinet is desirous of forming a new treaty with the Americans, and of converting them into useful allies, leaving tliem the masters of the new world, while Russia is to grasp the old, 'fhe policy of the Cabinet is to embarrass England in that quarter, as will be evident from the measures ordered since the ukase concerning the northern seas. A letter from St. Petersburgh of the 10th inst , again announces that Prince l'askewitsch will immediately proceed to Southern Russia ; and that Count de Witt will have an important command under the prince. The merchants of Moscow, in concert with those of Persia, have formed a company for depots of Russian merchandise at Bukore and Teffis, in order to compete with that of England, whose goods are conveyed to Persia thro' India, Erzerum, and Tabris. Tiiis company, it is thought, will have an immense influence over the commerce with Persia.

Wc learn by intelligence dispatched from the Hague, on the 23d inst, immediately after the business of the Chamber had closed, that the Second Chamber of the States General had just voted an address to the King in answer to his Majesty's Speech. (From the Morning Ihrahl) We subjoin the following extract, in substance, from a letter addressed by a gentle man of high standing at Bombay to a house of the highest respectability here, which was received by the overland mail on Tuesday, and which, as it refers to the aspect of political affairs in India, and t he sluggish administration of our foreign department, as well as that of tiie Board of Control, with respect to those important relations of the Biitish empire, will be read with some degree of interest : þÿ þÿ The public papers will have already informed you that we are about to make an attempt to close our north-west frontiers against tiie Russians, Persians, and Aflghans I trust that this effect has not been too long neglected ; and that we may be effectually prepared for tiie conflict which must ensue in that quarter. You may confidently mention that Lord Clate is in possession of a translated copy of an intercepted letter from a Russian officer at Caboul, to the Russian ambassador at Tcharan, in which the plans of the Autocrat are clearly developed ; and unless the details of what has taken place to which this letter refers to prove unfounded, your maudlin Lord Palmerston must have tiie veil removed from his eyes. þÿ Our relations w ith Nepaul are in a very equivocal state. It is stated that an embassy from tiie Nepaul government was stopped at Loadinaunat on the way to Herat, which cannot leave the object of that interruption in doubt. þÿ Tiie Burmese usurper is said to have

lowered his tone, but from his former conduct it is very questionable whether he is only temporising until our main forces are engaged in distant warfare. I must conclude bv saving that, during my long residence here, and certainly since the government of Lord Wellesley, the political horizon of India has never appeared so murky."

Heirs to the throne of France þÿ Our readers probably do not require to be informed that there is an individual now wandering about in Europe, calling himself Duke of Normandy, and claiming to be the legitimate sovereign of France by birthright. He maintains that the boy Dauphin, the son of Louis XVI, did not perish in the Temple, soon after the execution of his father, but that his life was preserved, and that the dead body exhibited was that of a substitute provided for the express purpose of facilitating the real Dauphin's escape, by creating a belief that he had perished, in the minds of those to

This soi-disant Duke of Normandy, now an elderly man, insists that he is the royal boy thus preserved by stratagem ; and be has been for several years engaged in preserving, but, so far, very unsuccessful efforts to establish bis claims to royal paternity, lie has, indeed, made some converts, who manifest a constancy of devotion scarcely exceeded in the annals of loyalty. For the last twenty years we have occasionally met with notices of bis movements and pretensions, and of the proofs by which the latter are supported : but as yet he has not succeeded in gaining his great object þÿ an interview with, or any notice from the Duchess D'Angouleme, (who, if he is really the son of Louis XVI, is his only sister,) although he has caused to be published numerous and minute details of events that took place in bis childhood, and by which, as they could be known only to herself and her brother, fie maintains that she must recognise him. lie has applied in turn to half the mouarchs in Europe þÿ not exactly for support, but for their inlluence with the Duchess, to gain lor him a hearing ; and he declares that Napoleon was so well satisfied of his identity as secretly to grant him a liberal pension þÿ instigated thereto, he says, by sympathy for his misfortunes, and perhaps by some undefined notion of using him, in some possibleemergencv, against his supposed uncle Louis XVIII. It fias often struck us as rather singular

that 'lie Duchess remains so obstinately silent as to the pretensions of this individual. þÿ The details he gives of his imprisonment in the Temple, of his father's words and actions throughout that imprisonment, and of little occurrences during his childhood, which could have been known only, it would seem, to the family of Louis XVI, are so minute and circumstantial that they appear to afford ample means of proving him an imposter, if be is one ; yet the Duchess will not speak cither for or against him ; she will neither admit nor deny the truth þÿof his statements ; and, as we have already said, lie has in vain solicited, for years, an opportunity of conversing with her, although he declares that, in a private interview, he can produce such oilier testimonials of his identity as must convince her testimonials of such a nature that he þÿ will not exhibit them to the world, but only to the person who alone can know their validity.

We did not intend, when we commenced this article, to enlarge so much upon the history of this pretended Duke of Normandy. þÿ Our purpose was only to point out the somewhat curious fact that, supposing his assertions to be true, there are now living no fewer than five heirs to the throne of France : the Duke of Orleans son, and the Count of Paris, grandson of Louis Philippe ; the Duke of Bordeaux, grandson of Charles X ; the soi-disant Duke of Normandy; and Louis Napoleon Bonaparte, nephew of the Emperor, and grandson by adoption, who claims as next in succession to the Duke of Kcichstndt. REMINISCENCE AND LETTERS OF NAPOLEON. In his report upon Corsica, lately read by M. Clanqui in the French Institute, he mentions a discovery lie had made of an early correspondence of þÿBuonapart s. He read a few of the letters, and merely alluded to the rest. It appears from them, that Buonapate, when young, studied with extreme closeness, scarcely allowing himself time to dress. One of his letters, at the commencement of the revoiutianarv troubles, is dated Auxonne where þÿ he was in garrison. He writes from thence; The drums beat I tremble lest 1 should be sent to Dijohn ; for it would cost me ten louia, and where the deuce am 1 to get then) ? One of his letters on the civil constitution of the clergy is verv remarkable, and, if known before, could not fail to have been quoted in our þÿ Irish polemics;-' A great þÿmistake, w rites be, to ask for oaths, for the stronger has no need of the oath of the weaker and the weaker w ho refuses becomes a þÿrebel. The following is a letter from Napoleon addressed to his lather from the school of Brienne, 1783 : þÿ My dear father, your letter, as you may imagine, did not cause me great pleasure, but the good of your health and family console and make me approve your return to Corsica And, indeed, whilst assured of the continuation of your kindness and exertion to push me on and second my wishes, why should I not be contented? I write, therefore, to ask what effect the waters have had on your health, and to assure you of mv eternal gratitude. 1 am delighted that Joseph has gone to Corsica,

provided he be here about the 1st November He may come, because Father Patrauld, my mathematical master, will not leave this. þÿ The principal bids me assure you that Joseph shall be well received M. Patrauld is an excellent master of mathematics; he will undertake to teach Joseph with pleasure, and if my brother will work hard we can go together to the artillery examination. You have no step to take in my favor, I being of the school, you must, however, for Joseph. But, as von have a letter for him, you say, that sudices. I had much rather you would send Joseph hers to Brienne than to Metz or any where else ; first because this would be a consolation to Joseph, Lucien, and me ; secondly, because you would be obliged to write and await the answer of the principal at Metz, which would be another cause of delay ; thirdly, they þÿdon t tench at Metz what Joseph wants for his examination in six months. My brother not knowing anything of mathematics, would be put in a mere þÿchildren class, s and disgusted. So that it is better to send him here ; and I hope to see Joseph before the end of October. Ho has no need of quitting Corsica before the 2Glh or g7th of October, in order to be litre the lgih or 13th of November. Send me. I pray you, Boswell's History of Corsica, with any other history or memoirs of that kingdi in. Don't be afraid but that I shall take care of them, and bring them back to Corsica, when 1 return, were it six years hence. Farewell, my father. Chevalet greets you : he studies

hard. The inspector will be here in a few days, and I will send vou word what he says to me. Present my respects to Minnanna Savcria, aunt Gertrude, uncle Nieolonio; compliments to Mannica Francesca Santo, Juana, Ignazio Send me tidings of them, and tell me they are happy. Wishing vour health as good ns mine, I am your very humble and most obedient son, De Buonaparte, Cadet.

From the New York Enquirer. FR1DAV MORNING, MARCH 1, 1839. Washington, Feb. 27, 1839. To the Houie of Representatives of the United States. 1 transmit to Congress copies of various other documents received from the Governor of .Maine, relating to the dispute between that State and the province of New Brunswick, which formed the subject of my Message of the 2 (5th inst., and also a copy ot a memorandum signed by the Secretary o! State of the United States and Her Britannic þÿMajesty s Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary near the United States of the terms upon which it is believed all collision can be avoided on the frontier, consistently with, and respecting the claims on either side. As the British Minister acts without specific authority from his Government, it will be observed that this memorandum has but the force of recommendation on the Provincial authorities and on the Government ot the State. M. VAN BUREN. MEMORANDUM Her Majesty's authorities consider it to have been understood and agreed upon by the two Governments that the tciritory in dispute between Great Britain and the United States, on the Northeastern frontier, should remain exclusively under British jurisdiction until the final settlement ot the boundary question. The United States Government have not understood the above agreement in the same sense, but consider, on the contrary, that there has been no agreement whatever for the exercise by Great Britain, of exclusive jurisdiction over the disputed territory, or any portion thereof, but a mutual understanding

that, pending the negotiation, the jurisdiction then exercised bv either party, over small portions of the territory in dispute, should not be enlarged, but be continued merely for the preservation of local tranquility as and lic property, both forbearing far as the pub- practicable to exert any authority, and when any should be exercised by either, placing upon the conduct of each other the most favorable construction. A complete undrestanding upon the ques tion, thus placed at issue, of present jurisdiction can only be arrived at by friendly discussion between the Gov rnments of the United States and Great Britain ; and, as it is confidently hoped that there will be an early settlement of the question, this subordinate point of difference can be but of little moment In the mean time the Governor of the Province of New Brunswick and the Government of the State of Maine will act as follows: Her þÿMajesty s officers will not seek to expel by military force the armed party which has been sent by Maine into the district bordering on the Aroostook river; but the Government of Maine will voluntarily, and without needless delay, withdraw beyond the bounds of the disputed territory any armed force now within them ; and, if future necessity should arise for dispersing notorious trespassers, or protecting public property from depredation by armed force, the operation shall be conducted by concert, jointly or separately, according to agreements between the Governments of Maine and New

Brunswick. The civil officers in the service, respectively, of New Brunswick and Maine, who have been taken into custody by the opposite parties, shall be released. Nothing in this memorandum shall he construed to fortify or to weaken in any respect whatever the claim of either party to the ultimate possession of the disputed territory. The Minister Plenipotentiary of her Britannic Majesty having no specific authority to make any arrangement on the subject, the undersigned, can only recommend, as ihey now earnestly do. to the Governments of New Brunswick and Maine, to regulate their future proceedings according to the terms hereinbefore sot forth, until the final settlement of the territorial dispute, or until the Govern-

ments of the United States and Great Britain shall come to some definite conclusion on the subordinate point upon which they are now at issue. JOHN FORSYTH, Secretary of State of the United States of North America, H. S. FOX, H B. M. Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary. Washington, February 27, 1839.

Interesting from Mexico. þÿ By the arlival of the Spanish schooner Bali/a, from Vera Cruz, which she left on the 23d December, we are in possession of intelligence confirmatory of the recent reports respecting a conflict between the French troops and the Mexican forces under the command of Santa Anna. The statement that the Mexican chief had been wounded, and had suffered amputation of the leg, proves to be correct. We learn in addition, that the city and castle have been evacuated by the French. þÿ Santa Anna has allowed eight days to the French residents in Vera Cruz for preparations for their departure, and sixty days have been accorded to the French in the interior for the same purpose It was currently reported that the Mexican government has resolved upon the expulsiou of all foreigners without exception. From the same source we derive information that part of the French fleet had removed from Vera Cruz, in order to renew the blockade of other Mexican ports. The corvette Creole, commanded by the Prince de Joinville, had gone to Havana on a cruise and there now remained hut four vessels of war before Vera Cruz. The Inspector of the Customs in Frederichsted, Kammerjunker and Captain in the Navy F v. Scholten Knight of the Legion of Honour has reported that in the Road of Frederichsted has been brought the Wreck of a Schooner Brig ANN, upon which excepting a Stump of the Foremast, were neither Masts, Anchors, Ropes or moveable Goods, and according to the Survey held, as far as regards the Outside of the Wreck, were on the Stern two Letters painted thus A: N: the Bowsprit cut off, a Bobstay chain about 4 lathoms, 3 dead Eyes with ironbands, 3 large dead Eyes to the chains abaft, with Ironbands on each side 4 do. do. w ith do. do. no Rudder, the Wreck is built of whilepine. With Regard to the Deck, it is 61 english feet long, 18 feet and 1 inch in breadth at the main Mast, 18 feet and 1 inches at the foremast, and 16 feet and 2 inches at the Stern and 10 feet in Depth at the pumps. The Main Hatch 26 feet and 2 inches long and 4 feet and 10 inches in breadth. The b'ore Castle Hatch 1 foot and 10 inches in J, the Companion way 4 (eet and 3 inches long and 2 feet in breadth. The Bulwark midships 1 foot and 9 inches, at the Stern 2 leet and 8 inches. In the Wreck were found standing 2 whitepine pumps, a Stump of the main mast, which was cut 3 feet above Deck, and found to be 19 inches in Diameter, 1 piece of the foremast was floating in the Hold þÿ a Part of the Deck cut up, the Vessel was waterlodged and in the Hold was found some lathes fit to receive stucco-work ; þÿ no Ropes, Sails nor

Anchors were found, and the Wreck to all appearance has drifted for 1 or 2 Years. The Goods landed of 1111 pieces of whitepine planks of 3 inches by nine, and from 10 to 16 feet in length. The Owner or Owners concerned in the abovementioned Wreck or Goods are hereby summoned in conformity with the Ordinance of 12th March 1790 and Royal Rescript of 2nd October 1822 sub poena precclusi et perpetui si ten tit, within One Year and Six Weeks from the day this Advertisement for the last time has been inserted in the Royal VVestindia Governments Gazette and the St. Thom Times, to appear before the undersigned Government and prove his or their legal title to the abovementioned Wreck and remaining Cargo. The Inspector of the Customs in Frederichsted, Kammerjunker and Captain in the Navy F. v. Scholten Ivnight of the l.egion of Honour has reported that in the Road of Frederiehsted has been brought the Wreck of a Schooner Brig ANN, upon which excepting a Stump of the Foremast, were neither Masts, Anchors, Ropes or moveable Goods, and according to the Survey held, as far as regards the Outside ol the Wreck, were on the Stern two Letters painted thus A: N: the Bowsprit cut oil', a Bobstay chain about 4 fathoms, 3 dead Eyes with Ironbands, 3 large dead Eyes to the chains abaft, with Ironbands on each side 4 do. do with do. do. no Rudder, the Wreck is built of whitepine. With Regard to the Deck, it is 61 english feet long, 18 feet and 1 inch in breadth at the main Mast, 18 feet and 4 inches at the foremast, and 16 feet and 2 inches at the Stern and 10 feet in Depth at the pumps. Thc- Main Hatch 26 feet and 2 inches long and 4 feet and 10 inches in breadth. The Fore Castle Hatch 1 foot and 10 inches in J, the Companion way 4 leet and 3 inches long and 2 feet in breadth. The Bulwark midships 1 foot and 9 inches, at the Stern 2 lest and 8 inches. In the Wreck were found standing 2 whitepine pumps, a Stump of the main mast, which was cut 3 feet above Deck, and found to be 19 inches in Diameter, 1 piece of the foremast was floating in the Hold þÿ a Part of the Deck cut up, the Vessel was waterlodged and in the Hold was found some lathes fit to receive stucco-work ; þÿ no Ropes, Sails nor

Anchors were found, and the Wreck to all appearance has drifted for 1 or 2 A ears. The Goods landed of 1111 pieces of whitepine planks of 3 inches by nine, and from 10 to 16 feet in length. The Owner or Owners concerned in the abovementioned W reck or Goods are hereby summoned in conformity with the Ordinance of 12th March 1790 and Royal Rescript of 2nd October 1822 sub poena praclusi d per petui silentii, within One Year and Six Weeks from the day this Advertisement for the last time has been inserted in the Royal Westindia Governments Gazette and the St. Thomie Times, to appear before the undersigned Government and prove his or their legal title to the abovementioned Wreck and remaining Cargo, The Royal Westindia Government St. Croix 29th of January 1839. J. SOBQTKER. David Hoskler.

From the St: Thomas Times, Feb'y: 1 3. HURRICANE AT LIVERPOOL. LOSS OF LIFE.

From our Private Correspondent. Liverpool, Monday Evening. Last night al 1 1 þÿo clockthis town was viited with a hurricane, which for the intensity of the fury with which it raged, and for the extent of the devastation it has entailed, has never been equalled as fat as the recollection of the most venerable residents can enable us to judge During the afternoon of yesterday the wind blew freshly from the southward and south eastward. Of this circumstance several out ward bound vessels availed themselves among whom were the Pennsylvania and the St. Andrew, the New York packet ships of the 25th of Dec and of the 1st instant. At 11 the wind in a terrific squall shifted to the northward and westward, from which quarter it continued to blow with the fury of a tvphon during the whole night. The morning dawned slowly and sullenly, as though it were afraid to disclose the extent of the dis asters which had signalised the gloomy night that had preceded it The streets were strewed with the fragments of stones, slates, and bricks, which had been hurled from the þÿroot a s nd dwellings. The houses, with their shattered windows, dilapidated walls, and broken roofs, presented the appearance ol a place which Itad recently been fiercely bombarded. The fury of the gale blew down at one swoop the wall of Kirkdale gaol. On the hanks of the canal a large cotton factoty had recently been erected, one wing of which was prostrated, and the cotton it contained scattered like flakes of snow in the neighbor-

ing district The handsome stone front of the Weslevan chapel erecting in Great Thomas street, the walls of which had but the preceding day been completed, fell with a terrific crash at four þÿo clock this morning Had the disaster resulted from the ignition of a subterranean mine, the masses of stone which have been displaced could not have been more thoroughly uprooted and widely scattered. þÿ The iron pallisades which guard, and the trees which did adorn, the grave yard of St. þÿJames Church, s are uprooted and overturned It is with pain we add that several persons perished in their bedsfrom the falling of chimneys. M rs. Lawrence, the mother of a member of the town council, was crushed beneath the weight of a stack of chimneys, which fell þÿ plump þÿdown, penetiating even to the cellar of the dwelling in which she resided. A Mr Marsh, who resided in the vicinity, has to deplore the loss of two of his children, who fell victims to a similar calamity ; and we are informed that upwards of 12 unfortunate beings have lost their lives in their own houses during the past night. As to the extent of the mischief which the hurricane has inflicted at sea, it is impossible to form an opinion. Premising that it will be difficult, until the accounts, which in the course of to-morrow we may succeed in obtaining shall enable us to estimate the extent of the misery of this disaster, we shall briefly append a summary of such facts as we have already succeeded in gleaning. The north-

west light ship was driven from her moorings and drifted into the river this morning. As if this calamity were not sufficient in itself to peril the fate and fortune of the vessels in the Channel, the Ridston telegraph pole was blown down ; and thus, at a crisis which requires prompt and certain communication;

BAiras TssTisransK all chance of maintaining it is cut off. Two steamers have sunk in the river. The basin of the þÿGeorge s Dock is covered with the splintered fragments of the sloops and boats, which have sunk or have been dashed to pieces. Thirteen vessels are on shore in Bootle Bay ; among them is the packet ship Oxford, her fore and mizen masts cut away, and with eight feet water in her hold. The packet ship Cambridge has drifted from her moorings, and is at this moment within one foot of the pier-head. Her commander has offered, we hear, 1000 guineas to any steamer which shall attempt to tow him to the opposite coast; no volunteer has hitherto accepted the offer. On the fate of the outward-bound packets we do not venture an opinion ; they are well built, manned and commanded, and we trust the excellence of their structure, and the ability of their captains, will enable them to reach a port of safety. Half past five o'clock. The gale is increasing, and brings with it a heavy shower ol sleet A boat, in attempting to reach the Cambtidge, which vessel has hoisted a sigi al for anchors and cables, upset, and five unfortunate men perished At this hour the gale is absolutely terrific. A dismal night, we fear, awaits us.

From the Burlington Gazette, December 21. SILK CULTURE. From the Norfolk Beacon. The cultivation of the Mulberry is not onlv j becoming a subject of great interest in the U. States generally, but in this immediate section in planting the Warns Vlulticaulus and snug of the country. Many are a I read v engaged . profits have already been realized We hail I its cultivation, however, as the first measure ' of introducing the silk manufacture among ns, and in establishing that branch of business firmly in our Borough. The soil of the neighboring country is admirably adapted to the rearing of the tree, while the town of Norfolk presents advantages for the location of factories unequalled we believe by anv other place in the Union. With proper energy and spirit, ; Norfolk might accomplish in the silk business what Paisley, Glasgow, Dundee, Birmingham and Manchester have done and are now do- S iug in other departments of industry Let it be remembered that the brisk linen manufacture of Scotland is from a raw material obtained front Russia, and ought we not to make an effort, with the mulberry and the sdk worm at our doors, to follow such a good example ? The silk business is destined to become one of the most important branches of \meriean industry. As late as 1795, England imported her cotton fabrics from India, and until the commencement of this century, imported all her cotton from Egypt and India. Companions in Arms ! þÿ Our country is in danger, and calls us to its defence. The government of a powerful and distant nation, which perhaps only knows us from the gold of our mines, and the treasures which many of its subjects have acquired among us, now insults us in every possible manner, and thinks it will civilize us though commencing by our degredation. It seeks our friendship to impose upon us disgraceful conditions by which alone we may be admitted to its amity, and because we have resisted nobly and justly, it has waged war upon our coasts. Our moderation and magnanimity, our desire to preserve peace, have been construed doubtless into imbecility and incapacity for self defence. In short we have been mistaken lor Algerines ; let us prove to them that we are MEXICANS. Valiant Troops ! Remember that you are tne same who, without foreign aid, without military tactics, even without chiefs, astonished the world by your heroic deeds, by your constancy in the combat, by your fortitude in enduring toil and fatigue: remember the resolution with which you plucked from the hands of your rulers the laurels of triumph, and brilliant trophies of conquest. Soldiers I þÿ The French have thrown down the guanllet in Vera Cruz þÿ it has been raised by some of our comrades, and the

maintain it, and let us swear on the altars of our injured country, taking Heaven and our posterity as our witness, never to lay down our arms until our rights are respected. Comrades ! In this sacred struggle we will constitute the vanguard ; our corpse de reserve will be the nation en mass, which admites our deeds, and will crown our victory or revenge our glorious death If the Mexicans in general, who cannot be indifferent to this title or to the national glory and honor, will follow our footsteps; and if the struggle to which wc have been so unjustly provoked should prove adverse to our cause, the vast territory of this republic will be converted into a single sepulchre ; the conquerors and the conquerred will be equally overwhelmed in it and an admiring world will say, þÿ The Mexicans no longer exist þÿ with them has disappeared their name, but it has vanished without spot or blemish ! Glory to so magnanimous an example! Shame to their unjust and haughty þÿaggressors,

Mi.k mc tJu) . «» Friends ! Let us flv to merit such enviable distinctions þÿ let us struggle unceasingly. Justice and the good wishes ot all who know and appreciate valor and the independence of nations are in our lavor. Your cause is not alone that of Mexico, it is that of the whole continent of every republican people, of all whom divine liberty is something more than-a name. All look to you with anxiety þÿ all ate eager to learn whether they shall term you their deliverers or shall load you with execrations. Who will doubt your choice '! There yet exists among you illustrious examples of those who led you to the combat, during the glorious periods when you achiev. ed your independence. A thousand others will rush to the fray, and all will emulate your indomitable valor. Mexicans, one and all. Your General the President, swears to you by his honor, that he will not be the last, and that linked with you, he will either share the triumph or seek a glorious death. ANASTASIO BUSTAMENTE. Mexico, Dec. 1, 1838.

j From the New Orleans Bulletin, Dee. 20. Important from Tampico. þÿ By a late arrival from this port we are in receipt of a letter dated the 8th instant, in which we give the particulars of an assault upon Tampico- The writer says þÿ Our city has had one of those hair breadth escapes from carnage, pillage and death, surpassing any instance known in the annals of the history of this country þÿ by an attack on the 30th ult., at 5 o'clock A. þÿM on one of the Forts. This attack was made by the infantry of Generals Canalizo and Cos, by their usual mode of intrigue, the advance guard entering the Fort and hallowing the usual cry of þÿ Viva La Federacion, Viva La General þÿUrrea They were received by General þÿUrreas and Montinegro's party as friends, but scarcely had their lips gave utterance to those unwished for sentiments, on the part of those who gave the griso, when the balance of these infuriated soldiers, were led on by the cheering cry of Cos, that the retail stores should be the fruits of their labor, as they should have an indiscriminate plunder of the same. This cry was reiterated from all the lines to inspire the troops to make successful charges, which they certainly did and obtained the summit of their wishes, so strife has now begun. Let us hasten to j far ns to gain the principal Fort, which commanded the town, and held it for two hours. The Federal party knowing, if those of the opposite took the town, that they had no hope of life, stimulated thus, they charged on them

again and drove them from the Fort with immense slaughter, taking General Piedrns and eighteen officers, and in all about four hundred prisoners, including killed and wounded. The loss of the federal party did not exceed fifty, including the lamentable loss of Colonel Montinegro, who fell in the early part of the battle. The accounts represent the attack on Tampico as quite a desperate and bloody affair. þÿ The Government troops, under Generals Co and Piedrns, were entirely routed, w ith a lot of five hundred men. The Federalist, under the command of General Urrea, defended the city with the obstinate bravery of men who have no choice between victory and butchery. They succeeded in enptut mg General Piedrns the commander of the Government þÿtroop:. lie was condemned to be shot, and the aeti-

tencc immediately executed. After the defeat the Government troops retreated some distance from Tampico, and halted to recruit and wait for reinforcements. From advices received by express, it seems highly probable that hostilities will be resumed, and regular war break out between France and Mexico The Mexican government has refused to ratify the articles of capitulation entered into before Vera Cruz, as signed by Admiral Uaudin and Gen. Rincon, and state that the whole country shall be made a spulchre boiore the demands of France are complied with. If this be a true report, we may anticipate the occurrence of important events in that quarter very shortly France will make quick work of it. aud count it no great task to enter upon the conquest of Mexico.

From the New York Daily Express, December 17, 1839. TMF. P \TRIOTS ROUTED t\D RUN AW \Y. The Detroit papers of the 5th and 6th give accounts of the defeat and dispersion of the whole patriot force The British loss at the attack upon tire Barracks is reported at 18, and several wounded. Patriot loss one (an officer) and three wounded The U. S. steamboats Erie, Illinois, and Macomb were cruizing in the river on Tuesday night and prevented þÿ any reinforcements crossing. Af- ter the þÿPatriots left Windsor they were pursued by troops from Malden, It is said they divided on their approach, part retreating to the woods and the remainder to an island in the river. The Erie, which was cruizing about at the time, arrested ten or twelve as they were crossing to the island, some of whom were taken before Judge Wilkins, examined and committed for utrial. þÿ From thirty to fifty escaped to the American side. On the approach of the Erie the main body of the British troops returned to Windsor, leaving a small force to pursue the party that retreated to the woods. þÿ The whole patriot force amounting to 250 men, were dispersed and routed by seventy militia men and six þÿregulars. Theller was arrested on Wednesday, and examined before Judge Wilkins þÿ gave bail for his appearance the next day. ilis trial will be postponed to next term. The Detroit Advertiser says, the most authentic report now is, that in the skirmish at Windsor, twelve patriots and eight British soldiers were killed. Up to yesterday morning the British had captured eleven prisoners,

some of them American citizens. Not a Canadian resident joined the Patriot invaders when they landed in Canada ! The whole number that crossed over, is stated by the Patriots themselves, to be two hundred and fifty.

EXECUTION AT KINGSTON. Col. Von Shoultz the Polo, was hung on Saturday week, lie was aged 31. Ilis father was a major in the Polish army at the battle of Warsaw. The prisoner also rose to be major in the Polish service. In 1836 he came to the United States, and settled at Salina as a chemist. Was induced to join the þÿ Hunters" or 11 Patriot Masons" by Mr. Stone of Salina, who also presented him with the flag that was taken at the Mill1 lie was told that the people of. Canada would receive them with open arms, and that even the Briish regulars would jo.u them on their land-

ing. Trusting to these representations ho embarked with others on the United States at Oswego, took the two schooners in tow laden with men, three cannon, and munitions ol war ; was baffled in the attempt to land at Prescott, but finally landed at the Windmill with þÿ180 men. He soon discovered how he had been deceived, as no aid came to them, nor did any one join them. But as he had no means of returning to the States, he strengthened his position as far as possible, and made the best defence he could Dorephus Abbey, a Printer, and second in command, was also to be hung on Saturday : also Daniel George, and Charles Smith, officers in the same expedition. Gov. Arthur orders the execution of all the prisoners convicted, and a number more were sentenced to be executed on the 12th.

We have to record one of the most awful and alarming shocks of Earthquake ever experienced in this Island, which occurred yesterday morning at a few nunutes before G o'clock. We were not in the least sensible of the shock ourselt, having been on horseback at the lime about 2 miles from town, but we find that the greatest terror and alarm was excited throughout the town, and all over die Island, from the long duration and awful shaking of the houses, and the noise as of carriages passing along the roads. Some are of opinion that this alarming convulsion ot the earth lasted 45, some think 50 seconds, and others a lull minute. The vibration we understand was from N. E to S. W. A few seconds more and every inmate of a bouse may have been buried in the ruins. Such an escape, by the mercy of an over-ruling Providence, at a moment when all thought them selves on the brink of a dread eternity, ought to excite the most devout gratitude, and lead to a serious preparation for a future and everlasting state. We have not heard particulars, but we are informed that several buildings have been þÿinjured. Barbadian, Jan. 12. þÿ o þÿ From the New York Gazette General Advertiser, Dec: 29, 1838.

Head Quarters Eastern Division, ) Cleavelano, Ohio, Dee. 10, 1838. \ " 1 was forced the ice to turn hack and by to laud at Huron, the 7th inst. þÿ reached De-
No. 632. Regierings Avis. MAN DAG EN den 21 de JANVARIJ I 39. .

troit the night of the 9th (140 miles,) and came here this morning (200 miles) in thirtyeight hours. " Brigadier General Brady's report to the Adjutant General of the Gth, will have informed you of the events which occurred at and opposite to Detroit two days before. The genera! results seem to have been that of the two hundred and odd patriots' who last crossed (the 4th) into the opposite province, thirty-seven were killed on the spot, and forty-eight have been made prisoners. þÿ A greater number escaped back to our shore, and a few wanderers remain to be picked up. It is known that the fugitives from the combat suffered much from cold and hunger, and that some of the prisoners are badly frostbitten þÿ the inhabitants refusing to give either shelter or food. " A small detachment of militia alone met and dispersed the invaders, with the loss of but a few individuals. " It may seem strange that this new outrage should have been committed near the United States authorities, both civil and miliary, without the previous knowledge of either 1 am, however, perfectly satisfied that the United States have not two more vigilant and determined commanders than Brigadier General Brady and Major Payne. As soon as the alarm was given, they, their officers and men, flew to the spot and exerted themselves to the utmost. The collector also did his duty, and the district attorney has been active in causing the principal offenders, who escaped to our shore, to be arrested."

Extraordinary Faculty. þÿ There is in the Philadelphia Institution for the Blind a pupil named Barras, who lias the uncountable faculty of computation so rapidly that you may ask him what was any day of any past year, or what will be any of years to come, and he answers you with perfect accuracy, almost immediately. For instance, you say, " Well, what day was the 29th of January, 18.30?" He tells you instantly. If you ask. " VV'hat day will be the 5lh of February, 1 N30 ?" again he answers at once. In fact, you can ask him no question which he will not promptly and correctly answer. And jet this boy never had the least instruction in mathematics to bring out his faculty. When he entered the Pennsylvania Institution he was regarded as almost an idiot ; he was deformed, being drawn down by the negligence with which he had been permitted for year9 to sit in the corner by the fireside in a state of absolute vacuity of mind. By the excel, lence of physical culture, he is now neatly erect ; and by the combined efforts of the benevolent leaders, he has also been astonishingly improved in his mental powers. How this boy makes his exact computation of time is not known ; but it is certain that he goes by some mathematical tide oi hit own. þÿ I'iuiad. Herald.

SILK CULTURE. We have been informed that a gentleman from New York is now extensively engaged cultivating in the Mulberry tree on this island, intending to ship it to the Northern Slates for the culture of silk They are of the species, Multicaulis, which was introduced into France from the Manilla Islands about eight years since, and is now cultivated in America to a great extent. The leaf is about one foot in diameter and is very tender and nutriiroos. The tree is easily cultivated, and of an uncommonly rapid growth. Doctor Wm. Stevens has raised in the Garden at Hogensborg one of a species called the Moretta, which in four Months has grown more than nine feet, and this species in the northern states grows with half the rapidity of the Multicaulis. Here where the climate is so propitious, the growth would no doubt be twice as rapid. In America the demand for these t:ees is great, and silk manufactories are establishing in every quarter. It has taken the more attention from the small degree of labour required. It is estimated that 3 women or children tor six weeks (the space of time the worm is engaged in spinning) can attend to 300,000 worms, 3000 worms will produce a pound of silk which is worth at the lowest estimate 4 Dollars per pound, which with a bounty of $ 2 50 pr pound that is given by some of the Northern States, would make 6 Dollars, thus in the short space of six weeks two persons, who may be in poor health, be incapacitated for heavy labour, will be enabled to realise 650 Dollars ; and it

may be enlarged to any extent. The House &c. for the use of the worms, require little expenditure, building a the size of a common Negro house, would accommodate a great number. The eggs have sold as high as forty dollars, and can now probably be bought for twenty five or thirty dollars per ounce, which will produce 30,000 worms. It is supposed that the exportation of silk from the Northern and Middle States, will soon equal that of Cotton, from the Southern If they make enough for their own consumption alone ; it would be much saved, as it is ascertained from official reports, that the amount of that article imported into the United States is twenty five Millions of Dollars annually. If such is the great profit to that Country, it must be still more profitable for this, when the climate is so agreeable, and the soil so fine, that the trees can be grown with the greatest ease, and instead of one, vera! crops can be obtaind during the year.

It would also give employment to those of our negroes, who are incapable of field labour. We understaad that one of our enterprising planters is cultivating the tree intending to grow silk on a large scale. He has written out for a large quantity of silk worm eggs, with a spinning machine &c. and we have no doubt that, with our advantage of climate and soil, not only he will succeed but that in a few years, the silk culture will be extended over our island, and will be equally with sugar a staple article to commerce.

From the Twenty-first and Twenty-second Annual Reports of the Sleswick- Holstein Bible Society, for 1836 and 1837. The usual intimation of His Majesty's gracious acceptance of the Sleswick-Holstein Bible Society's Report (being the Twentieth) was communicated by our Illustrious President, the Landgrave of Hesse, to the Committee, in a Letter given at the Royal Residence in Copenhagen, and signed by the King himself, under date of April 30, 1836. It was the last time that His Serene Highness enjoyed this pleasure ; for on the 17;h of August, the Venerable Prince was called away from his earthly labours ; & on the 30th of the same month his remains were deposited in the family vault in the Cathedral of Sleswick, on the day of his marriage with his august consort, exactly seventy years before. The age of the late Venerable Prince had greatly exceeded the general period allotted to man ; and his end was peaceful, and free from pain. His whole lite was marked by the most indefatigable exertion for the benefit of mankind, and of science ; but the favourite object of his labours was, to promote the extension of the Kingdom ol God on earth. He confessed the Name of Jesus both privately and publicly ; and never was he ashamed to own that he acknowledged Him as his Redeemer and Saviour: neither did he flinch from his testimony in behalf of the Gospel, even though he was attacked, and frequently misrepresented, by his infidel contemporaries. Thus he considered it as one of the happiest

moments of his life, when in early youth he had an opportunity, at the Court of Frederick the Great to declare, before a brilliant assembly, that he knew no higher happiness on earth than to be an humble believer in the Lord Jesus Christ The King of Prussia was silenced by the animated testimony of the young Prince, then attached to his service ; and it is remarkable, that, after a life devoted to the Gospel, lie was called away to see him face to face, on whom his soul believed, on the very day on which that monarch preceded him in death fifty years before. To the latest period of his existence, he considered it his highest privilege to labour for the glory of the Redeemer : and whenever opportunities occurred, he was not remiss in seeking to engage the co-operation of fiis high and influential friends. He was found, in his last moments, seated at his writing table, with his eyes half closed, and broken in death, apparently gazing on a painting of the (Saviour, which adorned his study. What he did, and what he projected for the benefit of the country, is matter of record for History : the remembrance of his zeal, in promoting the dissemination of the word of God, and the interests of the Sleswick-IIolstcin Bible Society, will ever be affectionate-

ly cherished in the hearts of all who had the privilege of being united with him in the same holy work. During the year 1836- 1837, the number of Bibles and Testaments circulated in the Duchies of Sleswick and Holstein amounted to 2815 copies. During the year 1837- 1838, there were issued, from the various depots in both Duchies 3187 copies of the sacred volume; making the grand total of the Distributions of the Sleswick-Holstein Bible Society, down to the present time, 80,488 copies.

The success of the Catholic Missionaries in India is chiefly to be ascribed to the examples they displayed of Christian charity in its most heroic degree. þÿ The Emperor of Japan called one day Father Necker who was at " Tell me in confidence, and I promise not hint, the head of the mission, and said to to betray you to any man, do you really believe in the doctrines which you preach ? 1 have called on bonzas and desired them to tell me sincerely what they thought of their own doctrines; and they have candidly confessed, that what they teach the people, is only a tissue of absurdity and falsehood, in which they do not themselves put the slightest credence. The missionary pointed to a terrestrial globe in the chamber, and desired the Emperor to measure the breadth of ocean which he had crossed to come to him, and then see what he gained, or had to gain, by the course he pursued. Your bonzas, "he added," are rich, happy and respected, and have every earthly good they can desire, I have abandoned every thing to come and preach these doctrines to you ; and tell me, is it possible that 1 would have undergone so much if I were not satisfied of their truthand of their necessity for you ?" Such an answer, was worthy of any minister of the Gospel of Christ. þÿ Quarterly Review, No. XII p. 3.

From the St: Christophrr Advertiser, Jan. 15. We are much concerned to loam, that a severe Earthquake was experienced at Martinique on Friday morning last, contemporaneously with the shock which was fell in this Town.

og Udgivet af Richard Hatchett. Every stone building in Fort Royal is said to have been totally destroyed. The exact number of lives lost had not been correctly ascertained, but 439 bodies had been dug out of the ruins, and it was feared there remained many hundreds yet buried. In St. Pierre, we hear that, happily, no lives have been lost, but a few buildings have been thrown down.

OyWe have been favoured with the perusal of a letter from St. Pierre, Martinique, which gives the following distressing particulars : þÿ " I have hardly a few minutes to mention to you the melancholy and dreadtul effects of an earthquake, at 5 minutes to G o'clock this morning þÿ one continued tremendous shake of about one minnte and a half's duration! demolishing some few houses here, killing and wounding some 7 or 8 persons, and so much injuring about 200 respectable houses, as to oblige them to be rebuilt. At Fort Royal, the Hospital, the Treasury, and most of the houses, crushed! þÿ burying about 500 unfortunate beings, of whom many dead, and many dreadfully wounded, have been disinterred ! ! On some plantations of which we have already heard the earthquake has demolished all the works. The main Church here is shut up as the steeple menaces momently a crush." It is verbally reported that General Bertrand was amongst the wounded at Fort Royal, and that he has since died. þÿ St. Lucia Free Press, January 12, 1839.

The LONDON GAZETTE of FRIDAY, December 14. By the Queen. þÿ A Proclamation. Victoria R. þÿ Whereas great numbers of evil-disposed and disorderly persons assem- lately, in some pans of Great Britain, have bled themselves together after sunset, by torch-light, in large bodies, and in a tumultuous manner, with banners, flags, and other ensigns, and have continued so assembled until a late hour of the night ; and during the time they were so assembled have, by loud shouts and noises, and by the discharge of lire-arms, and the display of weapons ol otfence, greatly alarmed the inhabitants of the neighbourhood of such assemblies, and endangered the public peace. We, therefore, being sensible of the mischievous consequences to be apprehended from such illegal meetings, and of the dangerous tendency thereof, not only to the peace of our kingdom, but to the lives and properties of our subjects, do hereby warn and command all persons to desist from such assemblies at their peril ; and do further command all justices of the peace, sheriffs, constables, and other peace officers, to use their utmost endeavours to prevent all such illegal assemblies, and to bring the ofiendors to justice. Given at our court at Windsor, this 12th day of December, 1838, and in the second year of our reign. God save the queen.

From the St Thomas Times, January 19. IT is our painful duty, to record the death of a distinguished fellow-citizen and a native of this place, PETER LOTHAhlLS DONS, m. d. aged 35 years, which truly lamentable event took place on the 16th inst. at 1 1 o'clock, p. m. His distressed widow has lost in him ail affectionate husband, who never sought his happiness beyond his family circle þÿ three young orphans a kind father, and those who enjoyed his intimacy, a friend, on whom they could reiy, for his judgments were founded on clear and impartial observation, and what he thought, and what he felt, he expressed wiih equal candour, whether in praise or in censure. No man was more averse to courting favour bv degrading arts, and yet, as a Physician, few are the men, whose mere entrance in the family, where his attendance was required, would produce the sigos of heartfelt satisfaction, hope and consolation, on every countenance, with which he was invariably received by young and old.' A strong sense of justice and duty, and a thorough hatred of every thing arbitrary and despotic ; love of science and truth in all its various branches, and contempt of vain and presumptuous ostentation, disinterestedness in a rare degree, honesty, generosity and benevolence of heart, formed the striking featuies of his vigorous and original character. Among the various pians of improvement, which occupied his mind, he used to dwell with particular fondness upon the devising some means for the more effectual alleviation of the sufferings and wants of the poor in

this island, especially during sickness, and the improvement of the hospitals, and if time had been spared him, no doubt some of his philanthropic designs would have been carried into execution. His mortal remains were interred on the 17th inst. at 5 o'clock, p m., attended by a numerous assembly, after an appropriate and impressive discourse by the Rev'd. Mr, Brondsted. He is now already enjoying the privilege of seeing clearly into those depths, which his searching eye endeavoured in vain to fathom, while among us. He dwells on high, far from and above die cares of a narrow-minded world. His memory will be cherished by the Poor, the Disconsolate, and bv all who had an opportunity of observing his excellent qualities. Eheu 1 Quanto minus cum rcliquis versari Quam liti mcrninisse !

Mr,- MMfT ifc a POET'S CORNER. -»»«K- TO BENEVOLENCE. Brightest gem of all adorning Human heart and human mind Many a woful heart this morning In gratitude to thee is joined.
Yea, and they have ample reason, For the goodness thou'st bestowed, During this inclement season, While it froze and while it snow'd.
Thou art a fountain overflowing With all that's good and great in nature ; Thou art a sweet star constant throwing Lustre bright o'er every feature.
Thy works are like the dews of Heaven Falling on the drooping flower; Life and health by them are given Through their sweet reviving power.
Oh ! the heart, not thee possessing, Ne'er to tender feelings yield ; Ought it know one earthly blessing? 'Gainst all fellow love' tis steel'd.
Heavenly gem ! mavs't thou continue Long to grace the breasts of those Who, from thy soft and tender feeling Mitigate the poor man's woes.
They in giving, feel a blessing, While their generous hands do bless; Where the weight of woe's oppressing, There they come to make it less.
Throughout the land thv balm be pouring O'er the wants of poverty ; Wretched hearts again restoring To their lost felicity.

Water Drinkers. þÿ There is a curious passage in one of Dr. Franklin's letters, in regard to wine ; he pleasantly observes, that the only animals created to drink water are those who from their confirmation are able to lap it on the surface of the earth, whereas all those who can carry their hands to their mouths were destined to enjoy the juice of the grape.

IBACT3JR TasrcirxaSR SafKKKftaSTQS AT'J3. Slave Mill at Sandwich þÿ Two thousand staves, fitted for the truss hoops, can be turned out in a day by three workmen, at the stave factory of Messrs. Stutson & Hoxie, in Sandwich. The machinery is propelled by water power, and consists of three circular and one cylinder saw. The logs are cut off to the length of a stave, by a cross cut circular saw ; they are then passed to the splitting saw, which divides them into slabs equal in thickness to the width of the stave. The cylinder saw which cuts the slabs i-ito slaves is the most complicated part ot the machinery of the mill. The saw resembles a large barrel open at each end, with teeth cut on the chimes It is placed horizontal, and revolves round an axis passing lengthwise through the centre of the cylinder The slab is fastened to a carriage which moves backwards and forwards on the same principle as the carriage of a common saw mill. All the workmen has to do is to secure the slab þÿ the machinery attached to the carriage gages the staves to a uniform thickness, and brings out the staves from within the cylinder as fast as they are cut off. The last operation is trimming, which is rapidly executed by a circular saw. The slaves made at this mill are superior to those made by hand. They are of uniform thickness, and are cut sweeping to conform with the shape of the cask þÿ the outside of each being convex and the inside concave, so that when put into heaps they form a perfect circle. The staves are principally re-
quired by the Boston and Sandwich Glass Company for packing their ware. þÿ 1 armvuth Register.

A BIT OF ROMANCE. A young man named Jones, was, some time ago, rescued from a watery grave by the intrepidity of a lady, a Mrs. Lee. Like a true Knight and gallant man, he felt himself bound to offer the lady a suitable reward. But we let the Lexington (Ky.J Intelligencer tell the story : þÿ A few weeks since we noticed the accidental drowning of four young men in the Lickins river, and the preservation of another, named Jones by the heroic conduct of a Mrs. Lee, who plunged into the stream, and succeeded iu rescuing him from the fate of his fellows. Mr. Jones, we learn, is a young man of fortune and accomplishments, and immediately after the event he made enquires respecting the preserver of his life, and ascertained that she was a young widow ; he offered her his hand in marriage, which she accepted ; and the parties were joined in wedlock the next Sunday þÿ three days after their first meeting in the water. Mrs. Lee, now Mrs. Jones, can congratulate herself upon having fished for a husband" with the " most entire success, and from the most laudable motives.

" It is, sir þÿ " One kind Kiss before we part." þÿ The gay youth, vaulting instantaneously over the table, saluted the fair stranger !

mmu ., vik ST. LUCIA, January 12, 1839. EARTHQUAKE. It has pleased the Almighty Disposer of events to visit us with one of those dreadful phenomena, which, whilst it surpasses the scope of human imagination to conceive, bespeak in the most awful manner the Omnipotence of the Creator. Yesterday morning, at 6 o'clock, a shock of earthquake was felt, of so severe and appallig a nature, as to baffle all description. It was unaccompanied by those premonitory rumbling sounds which generally usher in such convulsions. In a moment þÿ ere the most vivid presence of mind could have d;ctated any means of self-preservation to the numbers who at that hour had not stirred from their domiciles or their beds þÿ the roofs and walls of our habitations seemed ready to fall and crush all below them. Our senses were bewildered by the impetuous tossing motion of the buildings, as if they would be shaken up from their very foundations, accompanied with the creaking of roofs and rafters, and the crash of falling walls ; and we had no hope of afterwards beholding one house standing in Castries ! Lint the kind hand of that same Providence, from whose Mightiness proceeded the inexplicable phenomenon, was extended also to our preservation, in arresting the duration of the shock ere its effect had been the destruction of the whole Island It lasted about 35 seconds ; þÿ one second more, this town must have been in a heap of ruins ! In a moment, the streets were thickly studded with persons of all ages þÿ the helpless infant in arms, and the adult þÿ

numbers kneeling in ail directions, fervently supplicating for mercy. The damage done, as far as we have been able to ascertain, though extensive, we thank God is considerably less than our fears led us to expect. The Catholic Church of Castries, a fine new and substantial edifice, has been much shaken and rent in different places. þÿ Those extensive premises of Mr Muter, comprising the Council-Chambers, Court- House, and all the Public Offices, are most dreadfully split, and repdered unsafe. There is not a stone built house in the town that has not suffered, more or less. Amongst the worse, we noticed the following: þÿ Mr. P. Mallet's onestory house, which was for several years used as the Custom House; walls split in various parts, beams and rafters dislodged, aud Lhe eastern and western walls from top to bottom completely severed from the body of the building. House opposite l)r. Reddie's residence, corner of St Louis and Bridge streets, keystones dislodged cornices shaken, and wall so shattered, as to render it uninhabitable. þÿ House at the corner of Micoud and Bridge streets, occupied by Mile Suldeize Berland, cornices shaken off. and walls split, Madame Kosette Cools' new house, near the Square, western wall down ; and Madame Faget's roof crushed thereby. Madame Laffittc's shop, in St. Louis street, roof rent, and house thrown out about a foot on the pavement. þÿ The house of Mile. Siette Pattison, corner of Bridge street and Grande-rue, severely cracked and unsafe. Chimneys, tiles, and ovens,

thrown down in all directions. On Morne Fortune, the hurricane-proof iron barracks are split in several places. From Pigeon Island, the accounts are most dreadful, The two wings of the barracks are destroyed; the Officers' quarters rendered quite uninhabitable ; the inmates having nar-

Since our last the packet ship Wellington Chadwiok, arrived from London þÿ sailed from Portsmouth the 7th of December ; the United States, Holdiedgc, from Liverpool, sailed the 5th of December, and the steamer Royal William, from Liverpool December 15th, the latter bringing dates twenty days later than previous advices. Captain Swainson, of the Royal William, informs us that he took the southern passage, within a few miles of Madeira, and had theicby mild and comfortable weather the latter

" part of the passage. Although it is the first winter trip of the steam packet, the Roy al William performed admirably, and we understand the passengers speaking in high terms of the ship and her commander. disturbed state of the country. The torch light meetings in the manufacturing districts appear to have caused some uneasiness, as we find in the Globe of Dec, 14, a royal proclamation forbidding their repetition, &c. The Globe says that the getters-up of these meetings have wholly thrown off their disguise of pacific intentions ; that direct resort to violence is now preached by the orators : and quotes some very unequivocal expressions of O'Connor and Stephens. þÿ A mill at Manchester had been burned, in which 400 persons were employed : and no doubt was entertained that the building had been purposely fired. The owner, a Mr. Jowett, had incurred the ill-will of the " physical force men" by opposing the torch-light meetings. lord durham.

Lord Durham landed at Plymouth on the 30th of November ; and on the next day addresses were presented to him from the inhabitants ol that place and Stonehouse, in the town hall. It is observable that Sir Wm. Moles worth þÿ one of the ablest and most influential reformers þÿ stood with Lord Durham and his party on the platform, when the address was delivered. His Lordship was warmly cheered by about 1500 persons present in the hall address declared their approbation of his government in Canada. In bis answer Lord Durham declared his purpose to make in Parliament " a representation of facts wholly unknown in England, and disclosures of which Parliament and the people have no conception;" and that he should then " fearlessly demand from the Legislature that justice which neither they nor the people would ever deny to a public servant who had faithfully and honestly discharged the duties assigned to him. He also avowed himself an unchanged and unchangeable reformer. The London Spectator þÿ the able and powerful organ of the rational reformers þÿ although for some time past lukewarm if not positively hostile to Lord Durham, comes out openly as his advocate and friend. It considers liirn pledged by his speeches at Plymouth and elsewhere, as the advocate of triennial Parliaments, universal suffrage aud the ballot, and hails him therefore as the leader of the reformers. Mr. Stevenson had an interview with Lord Durham on the 10th of December. The Countess of Durham has resigned her

place of lady in waiting to the Queen, and the resignation has been accepted. This event is variously commented upon by the papers. It seems to be conceded, however, that it is the result of marks of disfavor shown to Lord Durham. The reduced state of the navy is exciting some uneasiness in England. Difficulty has been found in filliug up the complements of the ships already in commission, and it is conceded that under the present state of feeling the barbarous expedient of the press-gang cannot be resorted to. The mercantile marine is well and abundantly supplied but the naval service is said to be unpopular. Mr Justice Park is dead. Mr. Talfourd is spoken of among others, as lus successor on the bench.

The London Morning Chronicle announces that of the two millions of protested bills against the United States, sent out for collection by the Bank of England, all has been paid except t 400. The fact is the best answer to the abusive tirades of the London Times against the integrity of our merchants. The price of corn has again risen to the point which opens the ports to foreign grain þÿ the duty being only one shilling the quarter. (Jo apt Averaue. The dutv upon imported wheat was declared on the 14th of December, at the lowest point, namely, one shilling per quarter ; this will let out of bond all the foreign wheat under lock in the British warehouses, and induce farther importations ; and for this purpose large shipments of specie have been made to the continent. State of the Country. Fro m the London Morning Chronicle , Dec. 14. The state of the country is now become most alarming The recommendations of the men of violence are producing their natural effects. At Ashton-under-Lyne a factory, iu which nearly 40(1 people were employed, has been totally destroyed bv fire, arid the circumstances leave no room for doubting that the conflagration is the work of incendiaries. We are now arrived at a crisis which calls for prompt and vigorous action. In England, th ank God, the good sense of the people w ill not allow them to remain with their arms folded while the incendiary is applying a torch to their houses. FRANCE. Marshal Eobnu is dead, and Marshal Gerard has been appointed his successor in the

command of the National Guards of the department of the Seine. The funeral of Marshal l.obau was celebrated with great splendor. The whole garrison of Paris and the whole of the National Guard formed part of the procession, and. marching 10 abreast, were an hour and three quarters m passing a given point. The affairs of Canada occupy a large portion of the attention of the Parisian press. A paragraph is given in the Commerce, founded on a letter from St. Petei sLuiigh. iu which it is stated that at the late celebration of the Emperor's birthday at New Archangel, (the capital of the Russian colonics in North America), Admiral Count Kuprcseman, the commander in chief of the Russian naval forces on that station, gave a splendid banquet, at the close of which a collection was made for the unfortunate patriots of Canada. This collection, which (as Le Commerce observes) was in some sort official, and to which every body present, without exception, contributed, produced nearly 2,800f. (£112 sterling), and was forwarded to its destination by Admiral Kuprcseman himself. This statement, we may here remark, is gravely and feelingly commented on by the anti Russian portion of the London press, as proof positive that Russia sustains and foments the rebellious movements in the British provinces. RUSSIA. A strange story was going the rounds of the continental papers, to wit that the Emperor Nicholas has resolved to marry his second daughter to Louis Napoleon Bonaparte, and give hint Poland for his marriage portion.

®AiT3X T.83"J,aHJ>331t JsatHtatftinTDS AT33. who cultivate silk in the West Indies, and that three crops may he obtained in the year. A scientific gentleman, who has had much experience and paid great attention to the practical detail of the subject, states, we understand, that it only wants the encouragement of Government to make this island, as a silk nation, the richest spot on the surface of the Globe. Mr. Burke has, it is said, 300,- 000 Mulberry plants for sale. It must he very desirable for those who think of rearing Silk Worms to secure an early and ample supply of those plants. Some of the rich planters of this island might unite and send a small vessel to Monserrat for several thousands, to he immediately planted on their estates, for the purpose of feeding Silk W orms and raising silk for exportation, as well as for establishing a nursery of plants from which to supply their neighbours and their own future wants. There can be no doubt that the time has now arrived when all our energies should he aroused to develope and employ our resources, and when all available and profitable products for which the climate is suitable, but which have hitherto been neglected, must be introduced. It has, we think, become evident that capital will be more divided, and the number of proprietors increased, so that not many will be able to cultivate sugar and coffee to the same advantage as heretofore, and therefore will he driven to cultivate other and lighter products, such as can be managed with less labor and capital,

and that will give a greater proportionate return for the capital to be employed than either sugar or coffee will he likely to do in a short time. It would be well if some would at once turn their attention to the silk worm and the production of silk. We say at once, because if the worms are produced, the Ramoon would furnish food as Mr. Darker has shewed until the Mullbcrry plants are reared. Anything must he better now than the cultivation of sugar and coffee, when the trouble and the bother connected with their culture is taken into consideration, and it is only surprising that men of capital stick with so much pertinacity to those articles, to the total exclusion of all others. The questions as to the practicability and profitableness of rearing silk worms, have been so often before the public, that we almost feel loth to say anything more on them. We should be most happy indeed could we perceive some enterprising capitalist commence the experiment in right earnest, and with a determination to give it a fair trial þÿ St Thomas Times, January 9.
