LATER FROM ENGLAND Bv the arrival of the Ship Hibernia, Capt Cobu, yesterday morning, from Liverpool, whence she sailed on the 17th ultimo, we have Liverpool papers to that date, and London of the previous evening. The chief articles of interest in the English papers before us, have naturally relation to the disastrous hurricane, of which we received intelligence by the previous arrival. We extract so much of them, as the space we have at our disposal, will permit us to publish. It appears that the cargo of the Saint Andrew was in a better condition than had been expected ; the woollen goods were spoiled, but the silk and cotton were found to be in tolerable order. The cargo of the packet ship Pennsylvania had been seriously injured. and was exposed to plunder; the hull was entire, and the masts all standing at the last accounts. On board the passenger Ship the Lockwoods. the loss of lite has been dreadful. From the examination at Liverpool before the Coroner, it appears that shortly before dark, twenty-six out of more than one hundred per sons who were on board, were rescued bv the Victoria steam tug, but the greater part of the crew and the passengers were left on board during the whole of the awfully inclement night of Tuesday, when not less than 55 of them perished from cold, hunger, and exhaustion, amidst scenes of horror which no pen can describe or heart conceive 'J lie Victoria was again alongside the Lockwoods before daylight next morning, and rescued the

remainder of the passengers and crew. The high prices of grain have induced another strong and general effort throughout England in popular meetings, to procure the repeal of the Corn Laws The Chronicle and other ministerial journals appear to be in favor of material alterations in the present system ; yet when the powerful interests which are arrayed against the change are taken into consideration, it is very doubtful whatever may be the feelings of ministers on the subject, that they will tie able to obtain the sanction of Parliament to any modification of it. We have little doubt that Lotus Piiillippr under any circumstances will still command a sulficient majority in the Chambers to carry out his system of policy. I lis second daughter married to Duke Alexander of Win- TRMUuiiG died at Piza on the 2d January. Liverpool, January 15. Ever since the fatal morning of Monday week, the North Shore, strewed as it is with wrecked vessels, has been the scene of great attraction. Thousands upon thousands, on foot, on horseback, in gigs and coaches, visited it, and the beach presented a most animated appearance. The business of discharging the stranded vessels was carried on, particularly at low water, when the tide left tliein dry, with great activity, and the spectators around them, especially around the Oxford, were as thick as flies on a lump of sugar. As the hull of the Pennsylvania has, from the first, been under water at flood tide, her cargo is, of course, very seriously damaged,

while no small quantity of it has been plundered by the wreckers, who selected this fine ship as their especial prey. Twenty years have now elapsed since the first establishment of packet-ships between Liverpool and New York. During that long

'Jt'-SO'i'Jt'JUTOS ATU3« period, though the ships comprising the various lines have sailed in all weathers, both foul and fair, only three of them, up to the close of last week, had met with anv serious disaster. The Albion, from New-York for Liverpool, was some 18 years ago, totally wrecked on tfie Old Head of Kinsale, when the crew and passengers were drowned: the Liveipool, also from New-York to Liverpool, was subsequently lost, in the ice, on the banks of New Foundland, but every soul on board was saved ; and, later still, the Panthea was lost in Holy Head Bay. Since our last, however, three of these noble ships have been wrecked on our own shores, one of them, the Pennsylvania, certain to be a total loss, while the Oxford and the St. Andrew, though seriously damaged, may be repaired. We may state as a proof of the strength and admirable construction of the New York packet ships, that, though the Pennsylvania lias been lying in tiie surf on the Banks for six days, exposed to the beati»g of the sea, her hull was as straight yesterday as when it floated gracefully in smooth water; while that of the Oxford, which has been exposed for a day longer to the " pelting of the pitiless storm," in as staunch as it w as on the day she arrived from New York, the copper scarcely showiug a wrinkle. The St. Andrew's hull is in the same state The condition of these vessels, after their disasters, must give ere at O confidence to passengers in the safety and strength of the liners. London, 16th Jan. P. M. It is expected that considerable supplies of

corn will soon be obtained from various parts of the Gontinent. We learn by private accounts received from Paris, it was generally expected there that a partial change of the Ministry would take place. For these two or three days past a considerable improvement has taken place in the Portuguese Stocks þÿ and the cause, to the present time, is kept a profound secret. We hear that the rise in the above Stocks is owing to a negotiation now going on between our Government and that of the Portuguese, for the purchase of the Azores by the British Government, and for which twelve hundred thousand pounds have been offered þÿ Should this event take place it will fie a check upon the accumulating strength of the French in Africa.
